planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun to partial shade; this selection wants more elbow room than the species type.

directions: Fruitlandii is a larger-growing, more vigorous selection of thorny elaeagnus, prized for coarser, more heavily silvered foliage than the straight species and a broader, denser mounding habit that makes it a favored choice for tall screening hedges and windbreaks. Give it generous spacing since mature specimens can spread as wide as they are tall and will overtake nearby plantings if crowded. Like the species, it tolerates drought, salt spray, and poor or alkaline soils once established, fixes nitrogen through root nodules, and produces small, intensely fragrant fall flowers followed by tart, edible red berries in spring. Prune after flowering if a more restrained shape is desired, since it responds well to hard cutting back.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun for best gold color, though it tolerates partial shade.

directions: Maculata is the classic golden-variegated selection of thorny elaeagnus, each leaf marked with a bold splash of yellow-gold in the center that brightens through the growing season and deepens further in cold weather. Plant it in full sun for the strongest gold coloring; in heavier shade the variegation fades toward plain green and reversion shoots (all-green branches) are more likely, so prune these out promptly to keep the plant from reverting entirely. Otherwise as tough and adaptable as the species — tolerant of drought, salt spray, wind, and poor or alkaline soils — with the same fragrant fall flowers and tart edible spring berries. Its bright, evergreen foliage makes it a popular accent or hedge plant where a shot of year-round color is wanted.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun to partial shade for the boldest variegation.

directions: Gilt Edge is a widely grown variegated selection of Ebbing's silverberry, its broadly oval evergreen leaves edged in bright golden-yellow around a deep green center, giving a dense, colorful screen year-round. It shares its parent's tough constitution — thriving in lean to average, well-drained soil and tolerating drought, wind, salt spray, and coastal exposure that few other variegated evergreens can handle. Small, intensely sweet-fragrant creamy flowers appear in fall, followed by edible orange-red berries in spring that birds readily take. Watch for and prune out any shoots that revert to solid green, since these grow more vigorously than the variegated wood and will gradually take over the plant if left unchecked.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, lean to average soil; partial shade is fine but full sun brings out the brightest gold center.

directions: Limelight carries a bold gold-centered variegation pattern, the reverse of Gilt Edge, with each leaf splashed yellow-gold in the middle and rimmed in dark green, lighting up shaded corners and winter landscapes where evergreen color is scarce. Culturally it needs nothing different from the species type: lean to average, well-drained soil, tolerance of drought, salt spray, and coastal wind, and fall flowers so fragrant they can scent an entire yard despite being small and inconspicuous. Small edible orange-red berries follow in spring. As with other variegated elaeagnus cultivars, cut out any all-green reversion growth as soon as it appears to preserve the variegated form, since reverted shoots outcompete the golden growth over time.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
